kane-hall-polaris-009.description: Isaac Israel Hayes: Kane's surgeon on the Advance, who led the nine men that broke away in August 1854 and came back in December on Inughuit sledges with frozen feet; and, five years later, the commander of his own expedition to Port Foulke. Full-size original, 2296 by 3104 pixels.

kane-hall-polaris-013.description: Isaac Israel Hayes at his farthest north, from a cliff he took to be eight hundred feet high: 'all the evidences showed that I stood upon the shores of the Polar Basin, and that the broad ocean lay at my feet.' Of the water itself: 'A broad crack, starting from the middle of the bay, stretched over the sea, and uniting with other cracks as it meandered to the eastward, it expanded as the delta of some mighty river discharging into the ocean, and under a water-sky... it was lost in the open sea.' What Kane's man William Morton had reported from the Greenland side seven years before, seen again from the west. Hayes's latitude here is his own figure and is not accepted.

kane-hall-polaris-021.description: George Emory Tyson, the whaling master who kept the diary of the floe drift and got all nineteen people off the ice alive.

kane-hall-polaris-023.description: Tookoolito in her own tupik in Field Bay, having just produced a tin box of black tea and put the kettle on: 'I feel very sorry to say that many of the whaling people are very bad, making the Innuits bad too; they swear very much, and make our people swear. I wish they would not do so. Americans swear a great deal - more and worse than the English. I wish no one would swear.' One of the few places in this literature where an Inuk assesses the qallunaat rather than the reverse.

kane-hall-polaris-024.description: The elder Ookijoxy Ninoo, speaking through Tookoolito, told Charles Francis Hall of ships that had come long ago, and of five white men her people had taken who wintered ashore and built a boat. Hall wrote: 'Nine generations had passed away since the visit of Frobisher, yet now, on the 11th of May, 1861, I received from an old woman, probably a hundred years old, statements which I could not otherwise than believe to be facts concerning him and his co-adventurers!' She had described bricks, coal and timber on Niountelik, and ships coming in two, then three, then many - matching Frobisher's voyages of 1576, 1577 and 1578 exactly. Oral history holding for 285 years, and checked against the written record.

kane-hall-polaris-027.description: Ebierbing at the Starr Burying Ground, Groton, before going north again with Schwatka in 1878: 'he was observed to kneel at Hannah's grave and carefully weed out the long grass. Then turning to his visitors, he said, Hannah gone! Punna gone! Me go now again to King William's Land; if have to fight, me no care.' Hannah is Tookoolito, his wife; Punna is Panik, their adopted daughter. He had buried his wife and all three of their children. He went back to the Arctic and is thought to have died there about 1881.

kane-hall-polaris-032.description: The separation, from inside the Inuit families' camp on the ice, in the words of Hans Hendrik, who was there with his wife Merkut and their four children alongside Ebierbing and Tookoolito and George Emory Tyson. 'On perceiving this we brought our wives and children down upon the ice... Then the ice broke up close to the vessel, and her cables broke; but in the awful darkness we could only just hear the voices on board, and when the craft was going adrift we believed she was on the point of sinking. Here we were left, ten men, our wives and children, and the Tuluks, making nineteen in all, and having two boats, no boat remaining with the ship.' Tuluk is his word for the white men.

kane-hall-polaris-033.description: Hans Hendrik moving his family to the larger floe that became their island for the winter, his wife Merkut carrying the baby. 'My wife and daughter loaded the sledge with our little properties and pulled it, my wife carrying the baby in her hood. Our son was seven years of age, our youngest daughter four, and these poor things walked over the rough ice, my wife and daughter pulling the sledge, and I assisting those who dragged the boat - a sad sight.' Of the first night: 'But especially I pitied my poor little wife and her children in the terrible snow-storm. I began thinking: Have I searched for this myself, by travelling to the north? But no! we have a merciful Providence to watch over us.' The baby was Charlie Polaris, two months old.

kane-hall-polaris-040.description: The 198th day, in George Emory Tyson's journal. 'At 5 A.M., as I was lying in the boat, it being my watch below, but which had just expired, the watch on the look-out espied a steamer coming through the fog, and the first I heard was a loud cry, There's a steamer! there's a steamer! On hearing the outcry, I sprang up as if endued with new life, ordered all the guns to be fired... I also started Hans off with his kyack, which he had himself proposed to do, to intercept her.' Hans is Hans Hendrik, who paddled out to intercept the sealer Tigress of Conception Bay.

kane-hall-polaris-042.description: Charles Francis Hall, photographed at Washington in the winter of 1870, while he was lobbying Congress for the ship that became the Polaris. The only photograph of him known to exist. Full-size original, 1675 by 2061 pixels.

kane-hall-polaris-045.description: The grave of Charles Francis Hall ashore at Thank God Harbour, Polaris Bay, north Greenland, at about 81 deg 38 min N - among the most northerly graves in the world. The body was exhumed by Chauncey Loomis in 1968 and reburied.

kane-hall-polaris-046.description: The burial party for Charles Francis Hall at Thank God Harbour, 11 November 1871, in the dark of the polar night: they carried lanterns. A copper cylinder holding the history of the expedition was put into the grave. Full-size original, 3528 by 2176 pixels.

kane-hall-polaris-050.description: Hans Hendrik describing the shore that launched the open polar sea theory, where he stood with William Morton. 'This companion was named Mister Morten. We passed a great glacier, proceeded the whole day, and did not reach land before next morning. Again we went on, and fell in with a large open water. We followed the shore-ice, but when this ceased we were obliged to stop... The next afternoon we ascended the hill to build up a beacon, showing the point we had reached, and we marked the rock.' No polar basin, no dashing waves, no ocean: open water, the end of the ice-foot, a beacon, and a bear shot on the way. Set this beside Kane's account of the same journey.

kane-hall-polaris-051.description: Ebierbing - Ipiirvik, called Joe. Hunter, guide, interpreter and boat-builder on all three of Charles Francis Hall's expeditions and on the Polaris; the man Tyson credited with keeping nineteen people alive on the floe. He buried his wife Tookoolito and all three of their children at Groton, went north again with Schwatka in 1878 and is thought to have died in the Arctic about 1881.

kane-hall-polaris-052.description: Tookoolito - Taqulittuq, called Hannah. Interpreter, seamstress and guide on all three of Charles Francis Hall's expeditions and on the Polaris. She had spent two years in England from 1853 and dined with Queen Victoria; it was Tookoolito who told Hall on 6 December 1864 to be quiet and listen, which is how he got the Inuit testimony on Crozier. She survived the floe drift and died at Groton on 31 December 1876, aged thirty-eight.

kane-hall-polaris-055.description: A group photograph of the Polaris company, 1873, among them George Emory Tyson, the sailing master Sidney O. Buddington and the expedition's scientific chief Emil Bessels.

kane-hall-polaris-100.description: Two figures on one page from Charles Francis Hall's own sketches: the site where Inuit told Hall that qallunaat had camped, and the ice scraper a hunter uses to imitate a seal's noise.

kane-hall-polaris-156.description: The funeral procession for Charles Francis Hall over the snow at Thank God Harbor, 11 November 1871.

kane-hall-polaris-164.description: The moment on 15 October 1872 when the Polaris parted from the floe, leaving nineteen people adrift; the caption is a line from George Emory Tyson's journal of the night.

kane-hall-polaris-182.description: The track of the floe carrying George Emory Tyson and eighteen others from Smith Sound to the Labrador Sea, 15 October 1872 to 30 April 1873 - 198 days, and about fifteen hundred miles as Tyson's narrative reckons it.

kane-hall-polaris-183.description: The sealer Tigress taking George Emory Tyson and the eighteen others off the floe off Labrador on 30 April 1873.

kane-hall-polaris-194.description: Plan of Port Foulke on the Greenland shore of Smith Sound, drawn by Isaac Israel Hayes, where the schooner United States lay through the winter of 1860-61, with soundings and the shore establishments marked.

kane-hall-polaris-235.description: The expedition chart of Smith Sound and the Greenland coast from Elisha Kent Kane's narrative, showing the brig Advance's track to Rensselaer Harbor and the ground covered by the sledge parties.

kane-hall-polaris-243.description: The official chart of the North Polar Expedition under Charles Francis Hall, laying down three separate tracks in different lines: the outward track of the Polaris up Smith Sound to Thank God Harbor, her return, and the drift of the ice-floe party under George Emory Tyson that was carried some fifteen hundred miles south to the Labrador Sea, with the boat party's course.

kane-hall-polaris-119.title: Hall recovering Frobisher relics
kane-hall-polaris-119.description: Charles Francis Hall recovering Elizabethan relics on the Countess of Warwick Island, Frobisher Bay, during his first expedition. Inuit had known the site and its qallunaat remains for nine generations and pointed him to it; the plate's printed caption reads 'Hall discovering Frobisher relics'.

kane-hall-polaris-128.title: Ships of the Arctic search
kane-hall-polaris-128.description: A group of the vessels of the Franklin search, drawn together for the Polaris narrative; the plate's printed caption reads 'Arctic Discovery Ships'.

kane-hall-polaris-193.title: Map of Smith Sound showing Dr Hayes's track
kane-hall-polaris-193.description: The chart of Smith Sound with the schooner United States's track and the ground Isaac Israel Hayes claimed to have covered in 1860-61, drawn by Hayes and engraved by J. Schedler for his narrative. The sheet is lettered, in the book's own words, 'Map of Smith Sound, showing Dr. Hayes' track and discoveries'.

kane-hall-polaris-244.title: Coastal view from the Polaris
kane-hall-polaris-244.description: A tinted plate of the coast and ice from the official narrative of the Polaris expedition.

kane-hall-polaris-245.title: Ship and ice
kane-hall-polaris-245.description: A tinted plate of the Polaris among the floes on the passage up Smith Sound.

kane-hall-polaris-246.title: Ice cliffs on the Greenland shore
kane-hall-polaris-246.description: A tinted plate of high ice and rock on the Greenland shore of Kane Basin.

kane-hall-polaris-247.title: The winter quarters at Thank God Harbour
kane-hall-polaris-247.description: A tinted plate showing the shore establishment and figures at the winter quarters, with the Polaris housed over.

kane-hall-polaris-010.description: The scanned second volume of Elisha Kent Kane's narrative: the second winter, the treaty with Metek and the Inughuit, the abandonment of the brig on 20 May 1855 and the eighty-three-day boat retreat to Upernavik, with the appendices carrying the sledge reports, the meteorological registers and Kane's official letter to the Secretary of the Navy.

kane-hall-polaris-011.description: Isaac Israel Hayes's narrative of the schooner United States at Port Foulke in 1860-61, and of the sledge journey of spring 1861 on which he claimed to have looked out over an open polar sea. It carries the death of August Sonntag, the coordinates Hayes gives for Port Foulke, and his own farthest-north figures.

kane-hall-polaris-017.description: Compiled by J. E. Nourse by order of the Senate from the manuscripts bought from Charles Francis Hall's widow: the record of Hall's five years around Repulse Bay, 1864 to 1869, the sledge journeys to Fury and Hecla Strait and to King William Island, the Inuit testimony he collected there about Franklin's men, and the relics he brought back. Nearly all the wood engravings of Inuit tools, clothing, igloo plans and Hall's own sketches held in this layer are cut from this volume.
